Shemariah
shem-a-RYE-ah
n. (proper, a warrior who came to David; Hebrew, the LORD keeps)
Hebrew Shemaryah, from shamar, to keep or guard, and Yah — Jehovah has kept. Several men bear it: a Benjamite who joined David at Ziklag, and two of the men who put away strange wives under Ezra.

Biblical Definition

He is listed among the mighty men — Benjamites of Saul's own tribe, armed with bows and able to use both the right hand and the left — who came to David at Ziklag: “Eluzai, and Jerimoth, and Bealiah, and Shemariah, and Shephatiah the Haruphite” (1 Chronicles 12:5). Two men of the same name appear at the other end of the history, in the painful register of Ezra 10: “Benjamin, Malluch, and Shemariah” (Ezra 10:32) and “Azareel, and Shelemiah, Shemariah” (Ezra 10:41), among those who had taken strange wives and separated from them. The name is a confession that God keeps, and it is borne both by a man who left his tribe's king to join God's anointed while it was dangerous, and by men whose repentance was recorded by name for every later generation to read.

Origin & Era

Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a Benjamite warrior who came to David at Ziklag, and as the name of men in the register of Ezra 10.

KEEP, v.t. To hold; to retain in one's power or possession; to preserve; to guard; to protect.

PRESERVE, v.t. To keep or save from injury or destruction; to defend from evil; to uphold.

AMBIDEXTER, a. Using both hands with equal facility; as, the Benjamites who could sling stones with either hand.

DEFECTION, n. The act of abandoning a person or cause to which one is bound by allegiance or duty.

REGISTER, n. A written account or entry of acts or proceedings, for preserving and conveying knowledge.

Key Scripture

1 Chronicles 12:5 — "Eluzai, and Jerimoth, and Bealiah, and Shemariah, and Shephatiah the Haruphite,"

Ezra 10:32 — "Benjamin, Malluch, and Shemariah."

Ezra 10:41 — "Azareel, and Shelemiah, Shemariah,"

1 Chronicles 12:2 — "They were armed with bows, and could use both the right hand and the left in hurling stones and shooting arrows out of a bow, even of Saul's brethren of Benjamin."

Modern Corruption

A man's standing is judged by the company he was born into, where Chronicles records Benjamites of Saul's own kindred leaving him for David, at cost and while the outcome was still doubtful.

expand to see more

1 Chronicles 12:2 is careful to name the tribe: these were of Saul's brethren of Benjamin, armed with bows, able to use both the right hand and the left in hurling stones and shooting arrows. Shemariah was one of them. Leaving Saul meant leaving kinsmen, security and the visible throne for a hunted man in the wilderness with no guarantee of an outcome. Scripture consistently honours that kind of decision — Ruth leaving Moab, Moses refusing to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter — and it consistently costs something at the time it is made.

The other Shemariahs give the harder encouragement. Their names stand in Ezra 10, the list of men who had married strange wives and put them away — a register of failure made public and permanent. Both kinds of name are in the same Bible, and the same name is on both lists. A man may appear in the record of God's word as one who came at cost to the right side, or as one who sinned and repented at cost, and it is far better to be in the second list than to be absent from both because nothing was ever risked or ever renounced.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Shemaryah (H8114), Jehovah has kept; shamar (H8104), to keep or guard; Tsiqlag (H6860), Ziklag; badal (H914), to separate.

Hebrew Shemaryah (H8114) — Shemariah; Jehovah has kept or guarded.

Hebrew shamar (H8104) — to keep, to watch, to preserve; the LORD is thy keeper.

Hebrew Tsiqlag (H6860) — Ziklag; where the mighty men came to David.

Hebrew Binyamiyn (H1144) — Benjamin; Saul's own tribe, and theirs.

Hebrew badal (H914) — to separate; the act required in Ezra 10.

Usage

"“Eluzai, and Jerimoth, and Bealiah, and Shemariah” — men who came to David."

"“Of Saul's brethren of Benjamin” — what the coming cost them."

"“Benjamin, Malluch, and Shemariah” — the other kind of list."
